title: Anonymous Men Have Turned Cyberharassment Into a Group Sport—Here’s One Woman’s Side of the Story
gist: Podcast transcript in which WIRED's EJ Dickson describes the 'burnerverse', a loose network of anonymous college-sports burner accounts on X that doxes and sexually humiliates young women, using University of Florida student Maddie Kowalski's case (nonconsensual videos, #MaddieKowalski viewed 8.5M+ times) as the lens. It argues X's post-Musk algorithm and reduced trust-and-safety amplify such content, while police, universities, the Take It Down Act and misdemeanor-level laws offer only slow, limited recourse.

insights.claim: The 'burnerverse' is an amorphous, loosely organized community of mostly anonymous college-sports fan burner accounts on X, a segment of which is violently racist, misogynistic and antisemitic and systematically doxes young women.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Harassment is emerging from decentralized fan subcultures rather than organized groups, making it harder for platforms to moderate by account or network takedown.
insights.quote: It's unfair to even say network because it's just kind of an amorphous community of college sports fan burner accounts.
insights.locator: So, the burnerverse is a very loosely organized network

insights.claim: WIRED's reporting identified a little less than a dozen young women nationwide (late teens to early 20s, college students or recent graduates) who were doxed at viral scale by burner accounts after salacious rumors or nonconsensual images circulated.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: A repeatable pattern, not an isolated incident, raises the odds of regulatory and legal pressure on platforms hosting it.
insights.locator: So, there are degrees of it.

insights.claim: Beyond viral cases, burner accounts routinely dox on a smaller scale, reposting photos of incoming freshmen from college Instagram pages and screenshots of dating profiles alongside full names to mock the women.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Low-level, cross-platform exposure harassment is constant, implying persistent content-moderation and liability exposure beyond X.
insights.locator: But, the burner accounts were also doing this on a much smaller scale

insights.claim: In February 2025 an unverifiable campus rumor about Ole Miss student Mary Kate Cornett trended nationally on X after prominent figures such as Barstool Sports personalities and Pat McAfee picked it up, showing how burner-account content gets elevated into mainstream sports media.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Amplification by mainstream sports-media personalities converts niche harassment into national trends, a reputational and legal risk vector for those media brands.
insights.locator: So, I initially found out about the burnerverse in February 2025

insights.claim: Nonconsensual explicit videos of University of Florida student Maddie Kowalski went viral on X, with #MaddieKowalski trending nationwide and viewed more than 8.5 million times.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the reach X's trending system can give nonconsensual content, relevant to platform liability and advertiser brand-safety concerns.
insights.quote: #MaddieKowalski was trending on X nationwide, and it was viewed more than 8.5 million times.
insights.locator: The videos had officially gone viral.

insights.claim: The reporter believes this harassment would not have happened without Elon Musk's acquisition of X and its dismantling of trust-and-safety and content rules, because X's algorithm broadcasts divisive or inflammatory content nationwide regardless of subject.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Links X's algorithm design and moderation cuts directly to harm, strengthening regulatory and brand-safety arguments against the platform.
insights.quote: X's algorithm amplifies divisive or inflammatory content in such a way that it doesn't really matter what's trending.
insights.locator: Well, I mean, the platform didn't respond to me

insights.claim: X removed individual videos fairly promptly once takedown requests were filed, as legally required under the Take It Down Act, but takedowns are whack-a-mole because new reposts appear faster than they can be removed; X did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Reactive, per-item takedown compliance under the Take It Down Act does not contain viral spread, suggesting pressure for proactive detection mandates.
insights.quote: if you remove one, 10 more pop up in their stead
insights.locator: It's like a game of whack-a-mole.

insights.claim: When Kowalski reported the harassment, the Gainesville Police Department initially told her to change her phone number, and the University of Florida closed its Title IX investigation after about a month because there was no evidence the videos were filmed on campus.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Jurisdictional limits leave victims of online harassment with little early recourse from police or universities.
insights.locator: So, she had the presence of mind to go to the police department

insights.claim: Law enforcement and lawyers struggled because the case was not a typical revenge-porn case by an ex-partner but strangers in a network posting images of someone they did not know, with unknown account owners, motives and source of the leak.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Existing legal frameworks built around individual perpetrators fit poorly with networked, anonymous harassment.
insights.quote: the real chasm between the speed with which the viral news cycle evolves and the speed with which our legislation evolves
insights.locator: Yeah, I think that's what was confusing to law enforcement

insights.claim: It took Gainesville police a couple of months to subpoena X for account records, leading to charges against two Theta Chi freshmen and a former UF student for sexual cyberharassment, a misdemeanor carrying up to one year in prison and a $1,000 fine; one is alleged to have profited financially.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Anonymity on X can be pierced via subpoena, but light misdemeanor penalties may provide limited deterrence and fuel calls for tougher laws.
insights.locator: She ultimately decides to go after the burner accounts

insights.claim: Theta Chi said its chapter was on interim suspension and disavowed the members' activities after WIRED reached out.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Greek organizations face reputational fallout when members are tied to online harassment.
insights.quote: This is not what Theta Chi is about.
insights.locator: When I reached out to Theta Chi

insights.claim: Harassers were often the victim's own classmates behind burner accounts; they called her parents overnight, spread false HIV/AIDS claims, and bet on X whether she would start an OnlyFans or kill herself.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Harassment is local and participatory, which complicates the idea of it as a fringe or remote-actor problem for platforms and schools.
insights.locator: For the next 24 hours, Maddie sat paralyzed

insights.claim: Kowalski's sorority disavowed her immediately, reportedly holding meetings about how the incident reflected on them while members blocked and unfollowed her, which she saw as among the biggest betrayals.
insights.speaker: Zoë Schiffer
insights.so_what: Social institutions around victims can compound the harm, extending the long-term reputational damage.
insights.locator: I think she considered that one of the biggest betrayals
